notes: Friday 27 Nov 2026 world issue (Taipei ~08:00). Window: Wed 25 – Thu 26 Nov (US/Europe, Thanksgiving). Economy: US Q3 GDP revised up to 4.3%, Trump demands probe; Hernández de Cos to lead ECB; South Korea hikes rates; Norse Atlantic grounds flights. Tech: Nvidia chip sellers bar Chinese renters; S&P warns of Nvidia downgrade; Musk pledges SpaceX shares to US children; judge blocks FCC review of ABC licenses. Politics: Zelensky tells BBC US not pushing Russia hard enough; two Italians killed in Kuwait strike; Kim vows more nukes; Myanmar rejects parts of ICJ ruling. Literature (US): Woodward's Secrets; Lit Hub thankful list; Debs biography American Socialist; Capote's A Christmas Memory. Society: $40 HIV shot reaches Africa; Congo Ebola tops 12,000 cases; Iranian women protesters on death row; judge upholds Mamdani rent freeze.

stories.headline: US economy grew faster than first thought; Trump calls the fix a 'record setting error' and wants a probe
stories.dek: New numbers say the US economy grew at a 4.3% yearly pace in the summer, not 3.4%. Trump says the first number was 'fake' and hurt his party in the midterms. He gave no evidence.
stories.caveman: GDP is the total value of everything a country makes and sells. The US government first guesses it fast, using partial data, then fixes the number as more data comes in. On Wednesday, the Commerce Department said the economy grew at a 4.3% yearly rate in July–September, up from its first guess of 3.4%. On Thanksgiving, President Trump posted that this was a 'RECORD SETTING ERROR' that should be 'immediately investigated', suggesting the lower first number came out just before the November midterm elections, which Democrats won big. CNBC checked: the 0.9-point change is the biggest since 2020, but it is tied for only 16th largest since 1990, and the first number was already better than experts expected. The White House says the strong growth shows Trump's policies work.
stories.why_it_matters: Government statistics only work if people trust them. Attacking them without proof can make it harder for everyone, from businesses to voters, to know what is really happening.
stories.camps: Trump and his supporters say the early number was too low at a politically sensitive moment. Economists say revisions are normal and happen to every president; the original release was already strong. Some Wall Street voices add that a hot economy plus high inflation means the Fed is very likely to raise interest rates again in December.
stories.image_alt: President Trump speaks at the White House turkey pardon on Nov. 24
stories.image_credit: Photo: Aaron Schwartz / Bloomberg / Getty Images (via CNBC)

terms.explain: Gross domestic product: the total value of goods and services a country produces. The main way to measure if an economy is growing.
A correction to an official number after more data arrives.
Growth in one quarter, stretched out to show what it would be over a full year.
US elections held halfway through a president's four-year term, for Congress and many state offices.

stories.headline: Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos will be the next head of the European Central Bank
stories.dek: He will replace Christine Lagarde and be the first Spaniard to run the bank that sets interest rates for the countries using the euro.
stories.caveman: The European Central Bank (ECB) is like the Federal Reserve for the euro. It decides interest rates for the countries that use the euro, from Germany to Spain. On Thursday, EU governments agreed that Pablo Hernández de Cos, a former governor of Spain's central bank, will take over from Christine Lagarde. He beat Klaas Knot, the former Dutch central bank chief. It was a package deal: France's Laurence Boone and Germany's Markus Brunnermeier will also join the ECB's top board. France and Germany both backed Hernández de Cos, who is expected to keep the bank on its current path. EU leaders will make it official in December. Spain's prime minister Pedro Sánchez, who faces an election this weekend he is expected to lose, called it proof Spain is 'leading in Europe as never before'.
stories.why_it_matters: The ECB's choices change mortgage rates, savings and jobs for about 350 million people, and they ripple into world markets, including Asia.
stories.camps: Supporters say he is an experienced, steady pick who will not shake markets. Critics of these deals say top EU jobs are traded between big countries behind closed doors, rather than chosen in an open contest.
stories.image_alt: Pablo Hernández de Cos
stories.image_credit: Photograph: Rodrigo Jimenez / EPA (via The Guardian)

terms.explain: The central bank for the eurozone; it sets interest rates for countries using the euro.
A public bank that controls a country's money supply and interest rates.
The group of EU countries that use the euro as their money.
The small top team that runs the ECB day to day.

stories.headline: South Korea raises interest rates to a two-year high as its chip-powered economy booms
stories.dek: The Bank of Korea lifted its main rate to 3.25% and now expects growth of 3.9% this year and 4.1% next year.
stories.caveman: When an economy grows fast, prices can rise too fast. A central bank fights that by raising interest rates, which makes borrowing more expensive and cools spending. On Thursday, South Korea's central bank raised its key rate by 0.25 percentage points to 3.25%, the highest in two years. Inflation was 2.8% in October, above the 2% goal, and the bank expects it to stay high for a while. The big reason the economy is strong: computer chips. South Korea makes much of the world's memory chips used in AI. The bank raised its growth forecast to 3.9% for 2026 and 4.1% for 2027, and its governor said chipmakers' profits could reach 700 trillion won. He hinted that more rate rises may come.
stories.why_it_matters: South Korea and Taiwan both ride the AI chip boom. What happens there is a preview of the choices Taiwan's central bank faces: strong growth, but rising prices.
stories.camps: Supporters say acting early stops inflation from getting stuck. Others worry higher rates hurt households with big mortgages and small businesses that are not part of the chip boom, which can widen the gap between winners and losers.
stories.image_alt: Sign at the Bank of Korea in Seoul
stories.image_credit: Photo: Kim Jae-Hwan / LightRocket / Getty Images (via CNBC)

terms.explain: The price of borrowing money. Higher rates make loans more expensive.
When prices in general go up over time.
One hundredth of one percent. 25 basis points = 0.25%.
An official guess about the future.

stories.headline: Budget airline Norse Atlantic grounds all flights and may go bankrupt
stories.dek: The Norwegian low-cost long-haul airline says it will file for bankruptcy if it cannot find quick funding. High fuel prices from the Iran war hit it hard.
stories.caveman: Norse Atlantic flew big Boeing 787 planes on long trips, like London to Orlando, Cape Town and Bangkok, at low prices. On Wednesday it suspended every flight. It says it is talking to investors about a takeover, but if it cannot get short-term money quickly, its board plans to file for bankruptcy. A big problem: fuel. Many airlines 'hedge', meaning they lock in fuel prices in advance. Norse did not, so when the war involving Iran made fuel prices roughly double at one point, it was fully exposed. It lost $94.6m in the first half of the year. Passengers are stuck: one traveller in South Africa now faces an expensive ticket home. Consumer group Which? says not to cancel bookings yet, because that can cancel your right to a refund. Pakistan International Airlines, which rented Norse planes, also had to cancel UK flights.
stories.why_it_matters: Cheap long-haul flights are popular, but this shows how fragile the model is when costs jump. Travellers can be left stranded overnight.
stories.camps: Some say low-cost long-haul airlines are simply a bad business that keeps failing (like Spirit Airlines in May). Others argue the real cause is the fuel shock from war, and that passengers need stronger legal protection when airlines collapse.
stories.image_alt: A Norse Atlantic Airways plane
stories.image_credit: Photo: Getty Images (via BBC News)

terms.explain: A legal process for a company that cannot pay its debts. It may shut down or be sold.
Locking in a price ahead of time to protect against sudden changes.
Very long flights, usually over 6 hours, often between continents.
When one company or investor buys control of another.

stories.headline: Nvidia chip sellers tell cloud firms: no chips if you rent them to Chinese companies
stories.dek: A new US rule that started Nov. 19 closes a loophole that let Chinese firms rent top AI chips in data centers abroad.
stories.caveman: US rules already ban selling Nvidia's best AI chips to China. But Chinese companies found a workaround: they rented computing power from data centers in other countries, like in Southeast Asia, that use those chips. On Nov. 16 the Trump administration announced a rule to stop this 'remote access', and it took effect Nov. 19. Now, sources told CNBC, sellers are telling 'neoclouds' (newer companies that rent out AI computing) that they cannot buy Nvidia chips if any of that power will be rented to Chinese firms. Before, Nvidia's own line was no sales to customers renting more than half their chips to Chinese companies. Some sellers are now hunting for new buyers for chips first meant for those deals. Congress is also working on a Remote Access Security Act that would give the government even more power over cloud services.
stories.why_it_matters: This decides who gets to build the most powerful AI. Taiwan makes most of these chips, so the rules shape TSMC's and Taiwanese server makers' business too.
stories.camps: Supporters say the US must stop China from using American chips for AI and military use, through any back door. Critics say the rules are hard to enforce, hurt US and partner companies' sales, and may push China to build its own chips faster.
stories.image_alt: Nvidia logo
stories.image_credit: Photo: Getty Images (via CNBC)

terms.explain: Government rules limiting what products can be sold to certain countries.
A newer company that rents out AI computing power, often built on Nvidia chips.
Graphics processing unit: the type of chip that powers most AI today.
A gap in a rule that lets people avoid it legally.

stories.headline: S&P warns it may cut Nvidia's credit rating over 'governance' worries after the Huang drama
stories.dek: The ratings agency says Jensen Huang's ouster and return exposed weak board oversight and no succession plan.
stories.caveman: A credit rating is like a report card on how safe it is to lend a company money. Nvidia has AA, the third-best grade. On Wednesday, S&P Global Ratings put Nvidia on 'CreditWatch negative', meaning it could drop one step, to AA-, within 90 days. Why? Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang was pushed out and then brought back days later, amid questions about possible export-control violations. S&P said this showed problems with how the company is run: some board members have sat there since 1993, which may make them less independent, and there is no clear plan for who takes over if the boss leaves. S&P calls this 'key man' risk. Moody's, another ratings agency, had already lowered its outlook on Nvidia on Nov. 18.
stories.why_it_matters: Nvidia is the world's most important AI chip company and a huge customer for Taiwan's TSMC and suppliers. Trouble at the top can shake markets everywhere.
stories.camps: S&P says the company's money is fine, but the people in charge of checking the boss need fixing. Huang's supporters point to decades of huge results, and Huang himself told staff this week that Nvidia doesn't need a succession plan. A one-step cut would be small, but it can raise Nvidia's borrowing costs.
stories.image_alt: Nvidia logo on a phone screen with Jensen Huang in the background
stories.image_credit: Photo: VCG / Getty Images (via CNBC)

terms.explain: A grade showing how likely a borrower is to pay back debt.
How a company is run and checked: its board, rules and oversight of bosses.
A plan for who will take over if the leader leaves.
The danger that a company depends too much on one person.

stories.headline: Elon Musk pledges two SpaceX shares to every child in America, worth about $18bn in total
stories.dek: One share comes from SpaceX and one from Musk himself, going into the government's new 'Trump Accounts' for kids.
stories.caveman: 'Trump Accounts' are a new US government program that gives every American under 18 an investment account, to help them build wealth from a young age. The White House says almost 70 million have been opened. On Wednesday, SpaceX said it will put one new share into every active account next month, and Musk, the world's richest person, said he will add one of his own when his 'lockup' ends in June. At $127.44 a share, the total is nearly $18bn. Musk is worth around $824bn. Other rich people have done similar things: SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell gave shares to 2 million children. Rival AI company Anthropic, which went public this month, said it will set aside 5% of its shares (about $54bn) for a 'public good' fund.
stories.why_it_matters: Each gift is small per child (about $255), but it tests a new idea: giving every kid a piece of the stock market from birth.
stories.camps: Fans say it's a generous way to give ordinary kids a stake in big tech's success. Critics say it also links children's savings to one company's stock price, promotes Musk and a program tied to Trump's name, and is tiny compared with what taxes on billionaires could pay for.
stories.image_alt: Elon Musk
stories.image_credit: Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein / Reuters (via The Guardian)

terms.explain: A small piece of ownership in a company.
A US government program creating investment accounts for children under 18.
A period after a company goes public when insiders are not allowed to sell or move their shares.
Giving money to help others or society.

stories.headline: Judge blocks Trump's FCC from rushing a review of ABC's TV licenses, calling it a threat to free speech
stories.dek: 'This is not a close case,' the judge wrote. The FCC says the ruling is 'wrong on the facts and wrong on the law.'
stories.caveman: TV stations that broadcast over the air need a license from the FCC, the US agency that regulates TV and radio. Normally licenses are reviewed every few years. But in April the FCC, led by Trump pick Brendan Carr, started reviewing ABC's local station licenses early, years ahead of schedule, citing ABC's diversity programs. Disney, which owns ABC, sued. On Wednesday, Judge Loren AliKhan paused the early review. She said losing a license would be an 'existential' punishment, so even the threat can scare a broadcaster into changing what it says. She noted ABC had already changed how it handled guests on 'The View' and 'Jimmy Kimmel Live!' and how it covers Trump. ABC called it a win for the First Amendment.
stories.why_it_matters: Who controls TV licenses can control what news people see. This case tests whether the government can use paperwork to pressure the media.
stories.camps: ABC and press-freedom groups say the FCC was punishing a network for coverage Trump dislikes. The FCC says it is enforcing rules about fair hiring and the court got it wrong. Some note the judge was appointed by Biden, while the FCC chair was appointed by Trump. This is a temporary order; the full case continues.
stories.image_alt: ABC television network logo
stories.image_credit: Photo: Fred Prouser / Reuters (file, via CNBC)

terms.explain: Federal Communications Commission: the US agency that oversees TV, radio and phone networks.
Government permission for a station to use public airwaves.
The part of the US Constitution that protects free speech and a free press.
A temporary court order that stops something while the case is decided.

stories.headline: Zelensky tells the BBC the US isn't pushing Russia hard enough, and calls Trump's 'friend' Putin a killer
stories.dek: Ukraine's president says US delays on anti-missile weapons are costing lives, while peace talks have made 'no obvious progress.'
stories.caveman: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine is nearing its fifth year. Trump's envoys are trying to broker a peace deal, but the latest talks in Abu Dhabi went nowhere: 'The more we know, the more problems,' Zelensky said. In an interview in Kyiv, he said it was 'strange' that Trump posted a photo hugging Vladimir Putin and calling him 'my friend', because Putin is 'an aggressor, and a killer.' Zelensky said the US is too focused on the Middle East and is delaying Patriot missile-defense deliveries, while Russian missiles hit power plants and bridges and civilian deaths are at a record high. He said being 'very neutral' between attacker and victim is 'not right.' Trump, for his part, said on Thursday he had urged Putin to 'pull back all military aggression' in Europe and that a peace deal was 'a strong possibility.'
stories.why_it_matters: The war decides the safety of millions of Ukrainians and the future of Europe's borders. How the US balances friendliness with Russia against support for Ukraine is a key question.
stories.camps: Ukraine and many European leaders want more pressure on Russia and faster weapons. The Trump administration says it is staying neutral so it can broker a deal both sides accept. Russia has gone back to its toughest demands, so a deal still looks far away.
stories.image_alt: Volodymyr Zelensky speaking to the BBC in Kyiv
stories.image_credit: Image: BBC News

terms.explain: A person sent by a government to negotiate for it.
A US-made air-defense system that can shoot down missiles.
A fast missile that flies high in an arc before falling on its target; hard to stop.
Russia's all-out attack on Ukraine that began in February 2022.

stories.headline: Two Italian workers killed in a drone strike in Kuwait; Iran denies it was behind the attack
stories.dek: Kuwait and Italy blame Iran. Iran's foreign minister calls the incident 'suspicious' and a 'precooked recipe for war.'
stories.caveman: Since late February, the US and Israel have been at war with Iran, and Iran has fired missiles and drones at Israel and at Gulf countries that host US troops. On Thursday, two Italian technicians working for German arms maker Rheinmetall died after a strike on a facility in Kuwait. Kuwait said drones from Iran were shot down and falling pieces injured four people, including the two Italians, a Kuwaiti and a Pakistani. Iran says it did not attack: its military said 'no military or offensive operations' happened, and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi offered condolences and said Iran would help find out what happened. Kuwait called it 'heinous Iranian aggression.' A week earlier, Kuwait said it stopped Iranian drones aimed at an airbase used by US forces.
stories.why_it_matters: Every death like this raises the risk that the war spreads to more countries, which could push up oil prices worldwide, including in Taiwan.
stories.camps: Kuwait and Italy say the evidence points to Iran. Iran denies it and hints someone may be trying to drag it into a wider war. Investigations are under way, so the facts may still change.
stories.image_alt: A Rheinmetall facility in Kuwait
stories.image_credit: Photo: Reuters (via BBC News)

terms.explain: An aircraft with no pilot on board, controlled remotely or by computer.
Countries along the Persian Gulf, such as Kuwait, Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the UAE.
Sharp pieces thrown out by an explosion.
When a conflict gets bigger or more dangerous.

stories.headline: North Korea's Kim tours nuclear sites and vows more weapons, after ignoring Trump's offer to meet
stories.dek: State media showed Kim walking past rows of what look like centrifuges for making bomb fuel.
stories.caveman: North Korea already has nuclear weapons and keeps building more. During his recent trip to Asia, President Trump said he would like to meet Kim Jong Un. Kim did not answer. Instead, North Korea's state news agency said Thursday that Kim visited two factories that make nuclear materials, one brand new and one being expanded, plus a nuclear research institute. Photos showed rows of machines that experts think are centrifuges, used to make weapons-grade uranium, and halls displaying what may be warheads. Kim said he needs more nuclear weapons to deal with threats from the US and South Korea. Experts say he wants to show off his growing arsenal and make clear he will not trade it away in talks.
stories.why_it_matters: North Korea is a near neighbor of Japan and South Korea, and its weapons affect security across East Asia, including Taiwan.
stories.camps: Some say talks with Kim are still worth trying to lower the danger. Others say his message shows he will never give up nuclear weapons, so the focus should be on deterrence and sanctions. Note: these photos come from North Korean state media, which is propaganda and can be staged.
stories.image_alt: Kim Jong Un inspecting a nuclear materials facility, in a photo released by North Korean state media
stories.image_credit: Photo: Korean Central News Agency / Korea News Service via AP (via NPR)

terms.explain: A fast-spinning machine used to enrich uranium, the fuel for nuclear bombs and power plants.
Uranium enriched enough to make a nuclear bomb.
The explosive part of a missile.
Korean Central News Agency, North Korea's official state news service.

stories.headline: Myanmar's leader says he won't obey 'inappropriate' parts of the ICJ genocide ruling
stories.dek: Last week the UN's top court found Myanmar guilty of genocide against the Rohingya. Min Aung Hlaing says the word 'genocide' hurt the country's reputation.
stories.caveman: The Rohingya are a mostly Muslim minority in Myanmar. In 2017 the army launched 'clearance operations' in Rakhine State; the International Court of Justice (ICJ) found about 10,000 Rohingya were killed and over 700,000 fled to Bangladesh. Last week the court ruled, nine votes to six, that Myanmar committed genocide, the first country ever found to break the 1948 Genocide Convention. It ordered Myanmar to pay reparations, with the amount to be set later. Now Min Aung Hlaing, who seized power in a 2021 coup and is now president, says Myanmar will act like 'a responsible country' but will not follow parts it thinks are 'inappropriate.' He didn't say which. Myanmar still denies genocide and says soldiers were responding to attacks by armed groups.
stories.why_it_matters: If countries can ignore the world's top court, international law becomes weaker, and victims like the Rohingya may never get justice.
stories.camps: Rights groups say the ruling must be enforced, for example through sanctions. Myanmar's government says the army was fighting militants, not targeting a people. The ICJ has no police of its own, so enforcement depends on other countries.
stories.image_alt: Myanmar's president Min Aung Hlaing
stories.image_credit: Photo: Getty Images (via BBC News)

terms.explain: International Court of Justice: the UN's top court for disputes between countries.
Acts meant to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.
A mostly Muslim minority group from Myanmar's Rakhine State.
Payments to make up for serious harm done.

stories.headline: Hot: Bob Woodward's memoir Secrets, a 500-page ode to old-school reporting
stories.dek: The Watergate reporter, now 83, turns his famous digging on himself. The Guardian calls it 'entertaining, propulsive and juicy.'
stories.caveman: Bob Woodward is probably the most famous reporter in America. In the 1970s, he and Carl Bernstein at the Washington Post uncovered the Watergate scandal, which led President Richard Nixon to resign. His new memoir, Secrets, written with his assistant Claire McMullen, looks back at his whole career. He traces his urge to dig back to age 11, when he found out his parents' marriage was falling apart: 'You have to snoop, I concluded.' The book tells how he first met Mark Felt, the FBI man later known as the secret source 'Deep Throat', while Woodward was still in the navy, and how his first tryout at the Post failed. The Guardian's reviewer says the real hero of the book is 'shoe leather': knocking on doors, asking again and again, and really listening. It reproduces interview transcripts and memos, and admits he sometimes thought he was the cat when he was really the mouse.
stories.why_it_matters: At a time of quick hot takes online, a best-selling book about slow, careful reporting is a reminder of why journalism matters.
stories.camps: Fans see a master class from a legend. Critics of Woodward over the years have said he gets too close to powerful insiders and relies heavily on unnamed sources; this book is his own account of how those relationships worked.
stories.image_alt: Bob Woodward at the Washington Post
stories.image_credit: Photograph: Wally McNamee / Corbis / Getty Images (via The Guardian)

terms.explain: A book in which the author tells true stories from their own life.
A 1970s scandal over a break-in at Democratic Party offices and its cover-up, which forced President Nixon to resign.
The nickname of Mark Felt, the secret FBI source who helped Woodward and Bernstein.
Slang for reporting done in person, by going out, knocking on doors and talking to people.

stories.headline: Hot and not: what Lit Hub's editors are thankful for this year (small presses, yes; AI, no)
stories.dek: A Thanksgiving list from America's big literary website cheers small presses, booksellers and short books, and hopes AI's tide is going out.
stories.caveman: Literary Hub (Lit Hub) is one of the most-read book websites in the US. For Thanksgiving, its staff shared what they are thankful for in the book world. Hot: small presses 'and all the cool and weird things they're taking a chance on'; booksellers working through their busiest season; poetry archives from the Library of Congress; a short book you can read in an afternoon; Marilynne Robinson, called 'an autumn writer'; authors who take risks. They also cheered that the big book awards are 'no longer being afraid of support for Palestine,' noting National Book Award wins for Paradiso 17 and Huna. Not: AI. One editor is thankful for 'the tide continuing to turn against AI' and hopes its high-water mark comes soon. And the best feeling of all? A friend reads the book you recommended and tells you they liked it.
stories.why_it_matters: Lists like this show the mood of US literary culture right now: love for independent publishing, and growing pushback against AI in writing.
stories.camps: Many writers and readers share Lit Hub's worry that AI copies authors' work without permission and floods the market with cheap text. Others see AI as a useful tool and think the backlash will fade. The comment about Palestine reflects a debate in publishing too: some celebrate the awards' openness, while others feel prizes should stay out of politics.
stories.image_alt: Books with a Thanksgiving cornucopia
stories.image_credit: Image: Literary Hub

terms.explain: A small, independent publisher, often willing to try unusual books.
One of the top US literary prizes, given each November.
A person who works in or runs a bookstore.
A US holiday on the fourth Thursday of November, about giving thanks, usually with a big family meal.

stories.headline: Hot: a new biography of Eugene V. Debs, America's best-known socialist, lands as socialism is back in US politics
stories.dek: Shawn Gude's American Socialist tells how a young railroad union man from Indiana became a five-time presidential candidate.
stories.caveman: Eugene V. Debs (1855–1926) was a labor leader who ran for US president five times as a Socialist, once from a prison cell. Lit Hub published an excerpt from American Socialist: The Life and Legacy of Eugene V. Debs by Shawn Gude, a former editor at the left-wing magazine Jacobin, out from Simon & Schuster. The excerpt opens in Indianapolis in 1877: Debs, not yet 22, walks to the Indiana State House to give the opening speech at his railroad firemen's union convention, in a country still hurting from a huge economic crash. The book follows how he came to see the system of his day as 'despotic' and argued for a 'co-operative commonwealth', a democratic society built by 'the solidarity of ordinary people', not one great man. It arrives as democratic socialists like New York mayor Zohran Mamdani are winning elections.
stories.why_it_matters: To understand today's arguments about unions, workers and inequality in America, it helps to know the people who started them.
stories.camps: Admirers see Debs as a hero for workers' rights and free speech (he was jailed for opposing World War I). Critics of socialism argue its ideas don't work in practice. Note the author comes from the left; reviews will show how balanced the book is.
stories.image_alt: Eugene V. Debs giving a speech
stories.image_credit: Image: Literary Hub

terms.explain: A book about the life of a real person, written by someone else.
The idea that workers and the public, not just private owners, should share control of the economy.
A group of workers who join together to bargain for better pay and conditions.
A short piece taken from a longer book.

stories.headline: Still hot after 70 years: Truman Capote reads his own 'A Christmas Memory' in NPR's holiday tradition
stories.dek: NPR brings back the author's recording of his 1956 short story, now with a new illustrated comic adaptation.
stories.caveman: Truman Capote is the Southern writer behind Breakfast at Tiffany's and In Cold Blood. His short story 'A Christmas Memory' is about a 7-year-old boy called Buddy and his elderly cousin Sook, his best friend, in the rural South. Every November, when Sook announces 'it's fruitcake weather!', the two of them gather pecans, scrape together their small savings to buy ingredients, bake fruitcakes to give away, and cut down a Christmas tree. It is funny and gentle, but also sad, because it is about poverty, loneliness and a love that can't last. This week NPR again shared Capote reading the story in his own unmistakable voice, alongside a comic adaptation drawn by NPR's Jackie Lay.
stories.why_it_matters: Some books become part of how a country celebrates its holidays. This short story is a good way into classic American literature in under an hour.
stories.camps: Readers love its warmth and simple beauty. Some critics see it as sentimental. Capote's own life was complicated: brilliant, famous, and later troubled. The story is widely read in US schools.
stories.image_alt: Illustrated title art for 'A Christmas Memory' by Truman Capote
stories.image_credit: Illustration: Jackie Lay / NPR

terms.explain: A piece of fiction short enough to read in one sitting.
A new version of a story in a different form, like a film or comic.
A heavy cake full of dried fruit and nuts, a traditional Christmas gift in the US South.
Full of tender feelings, sometimes too sweet.

stories.headline: A cheap HIV-prevention shot, $40 a year instead of $28,000, starts arriving in Africa
stories.dek: The first generic lenacapavir landed in Zambia; Uganda is next. Two injections a year protect almost 100% against HIV.
stories.caveman: HIV is the virus that causes AIDS. There is still no cure, so stopping new infections is key. Lenacapavir is an injection given twice a year that is nearly 100% effective at preventing HIV. In a 2024 study of more than 5,000 teenage girls and young women in Uganda and South Africa, none who got the shot caught HIV. The original version, made by US drug company Gilead, costs about $28,000 a year in the US. Now a generic (a cheaper copy allowed under a deal) costs just $40 a person a year. The Global Fund says the first shipment arrived in Zambia on Wednesday, with Uganda next and Zimbabwe early next year. Over 189,000 people in 10 countries have already had a first shot, and the plan is to reach at least 3 million people by the end of 2028, working with the US government.
stories.why_it_matters: About 41 million people live with HIV, two-thirds of them in sub-Saharan Africa, and young women are hit hardest. A cheap shot every six months is much easier than a daily pill that people may hide or forget.
stories.camps: Health groups call it a 'major breakthrough'. But many worry that big US aid cuts under the Trump administration, including the shutdown of USAID, could undo decades of progress, because many African HIV programs depend on foreign money.
stories.image_alt: Lenacapavir injection for HIV prevention
stories.image_credit: Photo: AFP via Getty Images (via BBC News)

terms.explain: A virus that attacks the body's immune system. Without treatment it can lead to AIDS.
A cheaper copy of a brand-name medicine with the same active ingredient.
Pre-exposure prophylaxis: medicine taken before possible contact with HIV to prevent infection.
An international partnership that pays for fighting AIDS, TB and malaria in poorer countries.

stories.headline: Congo's Ebola outbreak passes 12,000 cases, the fastest-growing ever, as fighting forces aid workers to flee
stories.dek: Nearly half of those infected have died. There is no approved vaccine or treatment for this type of Ebola.
stories.caveman: Ebola is a deadly virus spread by touching the blood or body fluids of someone who is sick or has died from it. An outbreak declared in May in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo has now passed 12,021 confirmed cases, government data showed Thursday, and nearly half have died. It is the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak in history and Congo's deadliest, on track to pass the 11,000 deaths of the 2014–2016 West Africa outbreak. It is caused by a rare type, Bundibugyo, for which there is no approved vaccine or medicine. Stopping Ebola needs quick testing, isolating patients, tracking contacts and safe burials. But eastern Congo has more than 100 armed groups. New fighting near the city of Bunia has sent people fleeing, and about a dozen health workers, including two from the WHO, were trapped for three days in a hospital before being evacuated.
stories.why_it_matters: Diseases don't stop at borders. War, poor roads and distrust can turn a health emergency into a disaster.
stories.camps: Health agencies want more money and safe access for medical teams. Some residents distrust outsiders because of misinformation and years of conflict, which aid groups say must be handled with respect, not force. Both the army and rebels are being urged to protect health workers.

stories.image_credit: Photo: AP (via NPR)

terms.explain: A severe, often deadly disease caused by a virus spread through body fluids.
A sudden rise in cases of a disease in one area.
World Health Organization, the UN's health agency.
Keeping sick people apart from others so the disease doesn't spread.

stories.headline: Young women protesters face death sentences in Iran in numbers not seen for decades
stories.dek: Six women have been sentenced to death this year over January's protests, a UN expert says. Families describe beatings and forced confessions.
stories.caveman: Protests over the economy that began in late December grew in January into Iran's biggest uprising against its religious rulers since 1979. A US-based rights group says more than 7,000 people were killed in the crackdown; Iran's government says 3,117 died, including security forces, and blames the US and Israel. Now, rights groups say, women protesters are being sentenced to death at a rate not seen in decades. Twin sisters Taraneh and Romina Rahimi, 21, were arrested after joining protests. Their cousin told BBC Persian that Taraneh signed a confession after interrogators threatened to rape her sister in front of her; she was sentenced to death for 'moharebeh' ('waging war against God'), and Romina got 25 years. Both deny the charges. Others on death row include a civil engineer who drove injured protesters to safety and a 23-year-old convicted of blasphemy over a social media post.
stories.why_it_matters: The death penalty for protesters is one of the clearest tests of human rights. Women's voices from inside Iranian prisons rarely reach the outside world.
stories.camps: Amnesty International calls it a 'horrific rise' in political executions. Iran's embassy says the claims are 'misleading', denies torture, and says death sentences were for murder or armed violence, not peaceful protest. Court documents are mostly not public, which makes the facts hard to check.

stories.image_credit: Photo: supplied by family (via BBC News)

terms.explain: The group of prisoners who have been sentenced to death and are waiting for execution.
A charge in Iranian law meaning roughly 'waging war against God'; it can carry the death penalty.
When a government uses force to stop protests or opposition.
An independent expert chosen by the UN to report on human rights in a country.

stories.headline: Judge upholds Mayor Mamdani's rent freeze for about 1 million New York apartments
stories.dek: Landlords had sued to block it. The judge said the freeze had 'a rational basis', but also called the mayor's campaign slogan 'reckless.'
stories.caveman: About 1 million New York City apartments are 'rent-stabilized', meaning a city board decides how much rents can go up each year. Zohran Mamdani, a democratic socialist, won the mayor's race promising to 'freeze the rent' for these homes. In June, the city's rent guidelines board voted for a freeze on one- and two-year leases starting on or after Oct. 1. A group of landlords sued, saying the process was a 'sham' that ignored rising costs. On Wednesday, Manhattan judge Brendan Lantry threw out the case. He said his job wasn't to decide if the freeze was wise, only if it was reasonable, and it was. He did criticize Mamdani's slogan, noting that mayors can't freeze rents by themselves; only the board can. Mamdani said: 'Housing is not a luxury. It is a basic necessity.'
stories.why_it_matters: Rent is the biggest bill for most city families. This shows how a city can use its rules to make housing more affordable, and the fights that follow.
stories.camps: Tenants and Mamdani see a win for affordability. Landlords say freezing rent while taxes, insurance and repair costs rise will squeeze building owners and could mean worse upkeep. The landlords' lawyer says they are considering next steps, including a possible appeal.

terms.explain: A type of New York apartment where yearly rent increases are limited by a city board.
A rule that rent cannot go up for a period of time.
The New York City panel that sets allowed rent increases for stabilized apartments.
Asking a higher court to change a lower court's decision.
